title: Drawing lines, circles and filling regions
kicker: ENCT 201 · Computer Graphics and Visualization · Chapter 2 (output primitives)
subtitle: A screen has only whole pixels. These are the classic ways to choose which ones to light.

sections.title: The DDA line algorithm
sections.body: The DDA (digital differential analyser) steps along the longer axis one pixel at a time and adds the slope to the other coordinate, rounding each point: steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|), x increment = Δx/steps, y increment = Δy/steps. It uses floating point and rounding in the loop. From (0,0) to (4,2) it lights 0,0 1,1 2,1 3,2 4,2.

worked.why: Line from (0,0) to (4,2): Δx = 4, Δy = 2, so steps = 4.

questions.prompt: Why does DDA step along the longer axis?

choices.text: So the other coordinate changes by at most 1 per step and no gaps appear.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each step moves one pixel in the major direction.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — DDA from (2,2) to (13,8)
figures.note: Each frame rounds one point to a pixel.

sections.title: Bresenham’s line algorithm
sections.body: Bresenham keeps an integer decision (error) term saying whether the ideal line is closer to the pixel straight ahead or the one diagonally above. No multiplication or rounding: only additions and sign tests, hence its use in hardware. From (0,0) to (5,2): 0,0 1,0 2,1 3,1 4,2 5,2.

questions.prompt: The main advantage of Bresenham over DDA is…

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It is exact in choosing pixels.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — Bresenham from (2,2) to (13,8)
figures.note: The error term decides each step.

sections.title: The mid-point circle algorithm
sections.body: A circle is symmetric about both axes and the diagonals, so compute one octant (x from 0 to y) and reflect each point 8 ways. The mid-point method tests whether the midpoint between the two candidate pixels is inside the circle using a decision parameter p: start p₀ = 1 − r; if p < 0 keep y and p += 2x + 1, else y−− and p += 2(x − y) + 1. For r = 5 the first octant is 0,5 1,5 2,5 3,4.

questions.prompt: Why compute only one octant of a circle?

choices.text: Symmetry gives the other seven octants by reflecting coordinates.

sections.title: Filling: scan-line, boundary and flood fill
sections.body: Scan-line fill intersects each row with the polygon edges and fills between pairs of crossings (odd–even rule). Boundary fill starts inside and spreads until it meets a boundary colour; flood fill spreads through all pixels of the old colour. Both can use 4-connected neighbours (up, down, left, right) or 8-connected (plus diagonals); 8-connected fill can leak through a diagonal gap in a boundary drawn with 4-connected lines. The default pentagon fills 61 pixels.

questions.prompt: Which fill can leak through a diagonal gap in the boundary?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It also moves diagonally, through the gap.

figures.caption: Figure 2.4.1 — 4-connected flood fill
figures.note: The fill spreads from the seed to the boundary.

sections.title: Aliasing and antialiasing
sections.body: Because pixels are discrete, slanted lines look stepped (aliasing). Antialiasing reduces it: supersample (compute at higher resolution and average), or shade edge pixels in proportion to how much of the pixel the line covers. The cost is more computation.

choices.text: Renders at a higher resolution and averages down.

problems.prompt: A line has slope 0.3. Does Bresenham step mostly in x or in y?
problems.answer: |slope| < 1, so x is the major axis: x advances every step and y increases by 1 about 3 times in 10 steps.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• DDA: float increments; Bresenham: integers; circle: one octant + symmetry.
  • Fill by scan line, boundary or flood (4 vs 8 connectivity).
